identification.bodyShape: Elongate, cylindrical greenling body with one long, continuous dorsal fin running most of the body length, a large head, and a large mouth extending past the eye.
identificationTraits: A big mouth armed with about 18 large, sharp, canine-like teeth (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries).
A single long dorsal fin, rather than the separated spiny/soft dorsal fins typical of true cods (DFO, ADFG).
Scales cover the body but not the head (DFO).
Despite the common name, lingcod is a greenling (family Hexagrammidae), not a true cod (Gadidae) — no chin barbel and a different fin arrangement from cod (ADFG, DFO).
identification.coloration: Highly variable base color — gray, brown, green, or bluish dorsally — overlaid with dark brown or copper blotches and mottling in clusters, with a paler underside. Young fish show a more distinctly blotched pattern (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries, DFO).
identification.juvenileAppearance: Juveniles carry a blotched pattern and settle onto shallow nearshore sand, eelgrass, or kelp-bed bottom before moving onto rocky reef structure as they grow (NOAA Fisheries, ADFG).
identification.adultAppearance: A large, elongate greenling with a big toothy mouth, a single long dorsal fin, and mottled gray/brown/green/blue coloration over copper blotching. Females grow substantially larger than males.
identification.sexualDimorphism: Females grow faster past about age 2 and reach a much larger maximum size than males. CDFW gives maximum lengths of about 59 in for females versus 39 in for males; DFO similarly reports males rarely exceeding about 90 cm (living roughly 14 years) while females reach about 120 cm (living roughly 20 years).

similarSpecies.name: Other greenlings (family Hexagrammidae, e.g. kelp greenling)
similarSpecies.distinction: Lingcod is by far the largest hexagrammid, with a single long dorsal fin and a much larger mouth and teeth than the smaller greenlings it is related to. Agencies specifically flag that the common name invites confusion with true cod (Gadidae) even though lingcod is a greenling (ADFG, DFO).

identification.averageAdultLength: Commonly landed at roughly 24-40 in; maximum reported lengths are about 59-60 in for females (CDFW gives 59 in; NOAA Fisheries gives up to 5 ft/60 in) and about 39 in for males (CDFW).
identification.commonAnglingSize: Legal minimum sizes and bag limits are set annually by state and change with in-season action; see targetContext. Historically the recreational fishery has centered on fish in the roughly 22-30 in range.
identification.typicalWeight: Commonly a few pounds up to 20-30 lb in the fishery; fish exceeding 80 lb are documented by both ADFG and NOAA Fisheries.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 5 ft (60 in) and 80-85 lb (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries). California's oldest aged specimen on record was a 19-year-old, 45-in female (CDFW).
identification.longevity: Maximum documented age is about 25 years (ADFG, CDFW).

social.byLifeStage: Nesting males become strongly territorial for 5-11 weeks, guarding an egg mass in a rock crevice. Outside that window, lingcod are not documented schooling and show strong individual site fidelity to a home reef.
social.note: Tagging studies cited by CDFW and DFO show the large majority of mature lingcod recaptured within a few miles of their original tagging location — a sedentary, reef-holding species rather than a roaming or schooling one.

feedingStrategy.note: Described by every agency source reviewed as a voracious, aggressive predator that ambushes prey from bottom structure and takes almost anything it can fit in its mouth, including smaller lingcod (NOAA Fisheries, DFO).

behavior.territoriality: Territorial specifically around the nest: males claim and aggressively defend a crevice nest site for roughly 8-11 weeks (ADFG, DFO, NOAA Fisheries). Outside spawning, the species shows site fidelity rather than active territorial defense of a feeding station.

dielTendency.note: Diel (day/night) feeding activity is not clearly documented in the agency sources reviewed for this record; see gaps.

behavior.seasonalActivity: Fall migration onto nearshore rocky spawning habitat, followed by winter/early-spring nest-guarding by males, is the dominant seasonal signal. This is conservation context, not a targeting cue (ADFG, DFO, NOAA Fisheries).
behavior.depthMovement: Adults range from the intertidal to about 1,300 ft, concentrated in the 30-330 ft band; juveniles settle shallower over sand/eelgrass/kelp bottom before moving onto deeper rocky reef structure as they grow (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries, CDFW).
behavior.predatorAvoidance: Adult lingcod have few natural predators beyond marine mammals such as sea lions and harbor seals (DFO).
behavior.coverUse: Holds tight to rocky reef structure, and to kelp and eelgrass beds as juveniles (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries, DFO).
behavior.openWaterBehavior: Lacks a swim bladder and is consistently described as bottom-associated; open-water/pelagic use is not documented in the sources reviewed.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Migrates onto nearshore rocky spawning habitat beginning in fall; peak spawning runs early December through mid-March. Males establish and guard nest sites in rock crevices for 5-11 weeks until eggs hatch (hatching March-June); females deposit up to roughly 490,000 eggs and leave the nest site after spawning. This is conservation context only — nest sites and any pre-spawn staging habitat are excluded from target guidance (ADFG, DFO, NOAA Fisheries).

diet.primaryNote: Adults are aggressive, opportunistic predators. CDFW reports that fish make up about 80% (by volume) of stomach contents in larger individuals, with squid, octopus and crab filling out the diet; juvenile rockfish are an important prey item in California waters, and cannibalism on smaller lingcod is documented (NOAA Fisheries, CDFW, DFO). Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.youngOfYear: Pelagic larvae (roughly 3 months, early March to early June) feed on copepods and other zooplankton (NOAA Fisheries, ADFG).
lifeStageDiet.juvenile: Shifts to small fish, including herring, as juveniles settle onto nearshore bottom (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries).
lifeStageDiet.adult: Largely piscivorous — bottom-dwelling fish (about 80% of stomach volume by CDFW's estimate for larger fish), squid, octopus, crab, juvenile rockfish, and other lingcod (NOAA Fisheries, CDFW, DFO).

diet.preySizeShifts: Prey size and type track gape as fish grow, from copepods (larvae) to small fish (juveniles) to larger fish, cephalopods and crustaceans (adults) (NOAA Fisheries, ADFG).
diet.ontogeneticShift: Zooplanktivorous larvae, to juvenile piscivore on small fish, to adult generalist predator on fish, cephalopods and crustaceans — including cannibalism (NOAA Fisheries, ADFG, CDFW, DFO).
diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity is not proof that a particular prey event is occurring at a given time. Observed current forage still comes from a user observation or Hatch Match.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Lingcod hold tight to rocky reef, kelp and eelgrass structure year-round with strong site fidelity. The clearest seasonal signal is the fall migration onto nearshore spawning habitat and the winter-into-early-spring nest-guarding period by males, which is conservation context only. Depth-based closures, minimum size and bag limits are reset at least annually and vary by state — verify current rules before fishing.

entries.habitatClass: Nearshore rocky reef, as fish begin migrating onto spawning habitat.
entries.conservationNote: Pre-spawn migration onto nearshore rocky habitat begins in fall; this is conservation context, not a location cue (ADFG, DFO).
entries.presentationImplication: Bottom-contact and structure-vertical presentations worked tight to reef structure remain the reviewed nearshore families.
invalidators: treating fall staging behavior as a location to target

entries.habitatClass: Nearshore rocky reef and crevice structure, where males guard nests.
entries.conservationNote: Peak spawning runs early December through mid-March; males guard nests in crevices for 5-11 weeks. Some management areas add winter closures specifically to protect nest-guarding males (DFO, ADFG).
entries.presentationImplication: Where a season is open, bottom-contact and vertical-jig presentations on rocky structure remain the reviewed families; check season and depth closures first.
invalidators: fishing over an active nest site
assuming a winter season is open without checking current closures

entries.habitatClass: Nearshore rocky reef as the nest-guarding period ends and eggs finish hatching.
entries.conservationNote: Hatching continues into early spring (through roughly June); larvae go pelagic. This is conservation context, not a targeting cue (ADFG, NOAA Fisheries).
entries.presentationImplication: Bottom-contact, structure-vertical and vertical-jig on nearshore reef.
invalidators: treating late-hatching nest sites as holding water for adults

entries.habitatClass: General reef-holding on nearshore rocky structure and kelp/eelgrass edges, plus deeper shelf structure offshore.
entries.depthTendency: Adults spread across the core 30-330 ft band, with individuals documented from the intertidal to over 1,000 ft (ADFG, CDFW).
entries.presentationImplication: Bottom-contact, structure-vertical and vertical-jig nearshore; vertical-jig and deep-drop offshore.
